subject: Anthropology
title: Gender Across Cultures
description: Learn Gender Across Cultures in one minute.

hook.text: The Bugis people of Indonesia recognize five genders. The Western two-gender system is not universal.

buildup.text: Gender is the cultural interpretation of biological sex — the roles, behaviors, and identities a society assigns.

discovery.text: Margaret Mead showed that gender roles vary dramatically. What's masculine in one society is feminine in another.

twist.text: Many cultures have third genders: Two-Spirit in Native America, Hijra in India, Fa'afafine in Samoa.

climax.text: Gender is a cultural performance, not a biological script. Anthropology reveals its endless variation.

punchline.text: Culture writes the gender rules; nature doesn't.

quiz.question: What does cross-cultural evidence show about gender?
options: Gender roles vary dramatically across cultures

details.summary: Gender roles vary enormously across cultures, demonstrating that what counts as masculine or feminine is culturally constructed rather than biologically determined. Some cultures recognize three or more genders, while others assign roles that reverse Western expectations entirely.
details.whyItMatters: Cross-cultural gender diversity challenges claims that gender roles are natural and fixed. If cultures construct gender differently, then gender inequality is not inevitable but a product of specific cultural systems that can be changed.
takeaways: Gender roles vary enormously across world cultures
Some cultures recognize three or more gender categories
Cross-cultural diversity shows gender is culturally constructed

faq.question: What are examples of third or additional gender categories?
faq.answer: The Hijra of South Asia, Two-Spirit people among some Native American nations, Fa'afafine of Samoa, and Sworn Virgins of Albania all represent recognized gender categories beyond man and woman. Each has distinct cultural meanings and social roles.

faq.question: Does biology play any role in gender differences?
faq.answer: Biology influences average physical differences and hormonal profiles, but culture determines what those differences mean socially. The same biological traits are interpreted wildly differently across cultures, showing that cultural interpretation, not biology, determines gender roles.
